verses.text: When Rehoboam had come to Jerusalem, he assembled the house of Judah and Benjamin, one hundred eighty thousand chosen men who were warriors, to fight against Israel, to bring the kingdom again to Rehoboam.
But Yahweh’s word came to Shemaiah the man of God, saying,
“Speak to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all Israel in Judah and Benjamin, saying,

‘Yahweh says, “You shall not go up, nor fight against your brothers! Every man return to his house; for this thing is of me.”’” So they listened to Yahweh’s words, and returned from going against Jeroboam.
Rehoboam lived in Jerusalem, and built cities for defense in Judah.
He built Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa,
Beth Zur, Soco, Adullam,
Gath, Mareshah, Ziph,
Adoraim, Lachish, Azekah,
Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron, which are fortified cities in Judah and in Benjamin.
He fortified the strongholds, and put captains in them, and stores of food, oil and wine.
He put shields and spears in every city, and made them exceedingly strong. Judah and Benjamin belonged to him.
The priests and the Levites who were in all Israel stood with him out of all their territory.
For the Levites left their suburbs and their possession, and came to Judah and Jerusalem; for Jeroboam and his sons cast them off, that they should not execute the priest’s office to Yahweh.
He himself appointed priests for the high places, for the male goats, and for the calves which he had made.
After them, out of all the tribes of Israel, those who set their hearts to seek Yahweh, the God of Israel, came to Jerusalem to sacrifice to Yahweh, the God of their fathers.
So they strengthened the kingdom of Judah, and made Rehoboam the son of Solomon strong for three years; for they walked three years in the way of David and Solomon.
Rehoboam took a wife for himself, Mahalath the daughter of Jerimoth the son of David and of Abihail the daughter of Eliab the son of Jesse.
She bore him sons: Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham.
After her, he took Maacah the daughter of Absalom; and she bore him Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith.
Rehoboam loved Maacah the daughter of Absalom above all his wives and his concubines; for he took eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and became the father of twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters.
Rehoboam appointed Abijah the son of Maacah to be chief, the prince among his brothers; for he intended to make him king.
He dealt wisely, and dispersed of all his sons throughout all the lands of Judah and Benjamin, to every fortified city. He gave them food in abundance and he sought many wives for them.

footnotes.content: Rehoboam's first instinct was to use force—gather the strongest warriors and march against his own brothers. How often do we reach for power when we're afraid of losing it? He'd already lost ten tribes; his kingdom felt fragile.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God didn't argue with Rehoboam. He sent a word through Shemaiah the man of God—a quiet interruption. Sometimes the Lord speaks to us not through triumph but through a still voice calling us to stop.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice the address: Rehoboam the king, and "all Israel in Judah and Benjamin." God names the people as one. The split was real, but in His sight they remained His children, and He spoke to all of them through one word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You shall not go up, nor fight against your brothers." The command is plain and personal—and they *listened*. No one dragged them home; they chose obedience. The Lord's word alone turned back an army of 180,000.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After the war didn't happen, Rehoboam turned to building. He stayed in Jerusalem—not running to Egypt, not marching north, but settling into his inheritance. Sometimes faithfulness looks like staying put and strengthening what you have.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bethlehem was David's city, Tekoa would later know Jeremiah's pain—these were not random fortifications but places woven into Israel's story, places where the Lord had moved before.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Beth Zur, Adullam—Adullam was where David fled when hunted. Rehoboam built in the places of old refuge, as if learning from the past that God's people survive through strongholds of faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Each city named had watched Israel's history unfold. Mareshah would see war and deliverance; Gath had known David's sorrows. Rehoboam built in places already sanctified by the faithfulness of his ancestors.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lachish, Azekah—strongholds that would stand through siege and calamity. Rehoboam was building not just walls but a defense that would shelter his people for generations, even when he was long gone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten cities across Judah and Benjamin, "exceedingly strong." Rehoboam wasn't hoarding power; he was distributing strength—the mark of a ruler learning that true defense rests on many strongholds, not one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Stores of food, oil and wine"—he provided for his cities not just with weapons but with what sustains life. A good steward prepares both for war and for everyday mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Made them exceedingly strong." The text emphasizes it twice: he did the work thoroughly. Judah and Benjamin belonged to him not by conquest but by provision and care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priests and Levites came "out of all their territory." They chose to leave the north and serve in Jerusalem, in Rehoboam's kingdom. Sometimes faithfulness draws others toward faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam cast them off so they wouldn't execute the priest's office to the Lord—he feared their faithfulness more than their numbers. Rehoboam received them gladly. The king who hears God's word draws the faithful near.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A dark turn: Jeroboam "appointed priests for the high places, for the male goats, and for the calves." Political power without faithfulness to the Lord becomes a drift into idolatry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Those who set their hearts to seek Yahweh came to Jerusalem to sacrifice." It names the true migration: not refugees fleeing, but seekers choosing the place where they could worship the true God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "For three years they walked in the way of David and Solomon." Rehoboam's kingdom was strengthened not by armies alone but by a people aligned with the ways of their faithful ancestors. Faithfulness to the past wisdom made them strong.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rehoboam took Mahalath, tracing her lineage through David and Jesse. Even in his marriages he was binding himself to the house's faithful bloodline.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three sons from Mahalath: Jeush, Shemariah, Zaham. Each name carried hope that the kingdom might find stability through the next generation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then Maacah, daughter of Absalom. She bore him four more sons, binding him to another line of David's descendants—but Absalom had tried to overthrow David. Sometimes we inherit complexity along with blood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rehoboam loved Maacah above the others, and took eighteen wives and sixty concubines. This sprawl of household—twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters—would fragment his legacy just as Jeroboam's apostasy had fragmented the kingdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He appointed Abijah, Maacah's son, to be chief. Choosing one son to lead meant loving one more than others—a kindness to Abijah but a sorrow for the rest, and a fracture waiting to open.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He dispersed his sons throughout the fortified cities "and sought many wives for them"—a practical care, but it scattered his house just as the kingdom itself was scattered. Readers today hear an echo: power without a unifying center becomes fragmentation, no matter how well-provisioned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
